utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Today we will continue with our work. Registrar, would you please call out the number of the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14/1-T, Prosecutor against Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Appearances, please. For the Prosecution, Mr. Neimann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic and I represent the Defence together with my colleague, Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We have a long day today. In order to organise ourselves, I will tell you that we have to have a break at 10.00 because we have the Deputy -- the Chief Registrar here, so we will work until 10.00, and then we will have a break of ten minutes, then we will continue at 10.40 until noon. After that, we will have a 20-minute break until 12.20, until 13.30, then we will have a break of ten minutes and we will work from 13.40 until 2.15, as I announced yesterday. Is this okay? Good day to our simultaneous interpreters, the technicians. Is everybody ready? Yes. Okay. In that case, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I wonder if there has been a mis-translation because Your Honours I think said that we would have a break at 10.00 for ten minutes and then continue at 10.40, which wouldn't be right, if that was the case. Did Your Honour say longer than ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Of 40 minutes, from 9.00 to 10.00. Yes, 40 minutes. Thank you very much. JUDGE NIETO NAVIA: Just for the record, the meeting at 10.00 is with the Under Secretary General of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let it go in the record that the 10.00 meeting ... of the Secretary General of the United Nations and then we will make a 10-minute break. Good day, Professor Bilandzic, and Mr. Mikulicic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my learned colleagues of the Prosecution, and Professor, good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today we will continue with your testimony, and we will pick up where we left off yesterday. Professor, yesterday you started on the subject that in the history of the territory of the former Yugoslavia is known as the happening of the people. These were mass gatherings of the population in certain parts of the Republic of Serbia and the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, and you started to talk about who organised those gatherings and for what purpose. So please, would you continue your testimony from there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: The social processes, as you know, are often hidden, the forces which are preparing social processes often come out with false slogans and false manipulative ideas. The "happening of the people" in the beginning was conceived as a movement of democratic, i.e. this movement was supposed to topple bureaucratic structures which lasted for 40 years so that a new cultural revolution would bring in fresh blood by destroying old structures. However, it quickly turned into -- very, very quickly turned into an all Serbian national movement which quickly reached the very last village, the very last man in Serbia, in Bosnia, and Croatia, so that we could say that somewhere around 1988, 1989, a Pan-Serbian national movement was formed in order to save Yugoslavia and Communism. Milosevic, at one moment in that heated atmosphere, stated that force will have to be used and perhaps even war in order to save Communism and Yugoslavia. I personally think, even though we are here broaching a subject that is not really a part of historiography because we don't have the distance. As a historian, as a rule, I wouldn't, according to rules of science, I really wouldn't be able to go into this because there is no time distance. But I think that the military leadership and the Serbian leadership thought that they would achieve their goals without war. Why? In 1988-1989, the advantages on the side of the military leadership and Serbia were frightening in relation to their political opponents, meaning the military leadership. Serbia had at their disposal four or five instruments which were very powerful. First, as I said, Serbs in the whole of Yugoslavia were in a national euphoria, and they were united to a man. Also, they had the JNA, the Yugoslav army, which was ready ideologically to defend the two supreme human values, and these were Communism and Yugoslavia, they were ready to defend that. The person who has the army on his side and the military leadership, and Serbia thought they had the army on their side, could count -- they could rule Yugoslavia. The third factor which was in the hands of the military and Serbian leadership was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. The League of Communists of Yugoslavia was the ruling party, and they have the greatest influence and power in that party, and that person can easily rule Yugoslavia. The next factor is the international community, the East and the West were very interested to maintain, to preserve Yugoslavia, so they could count Milosevic and the military leadership could count on the solidarity of the international community. Not to them as people, not Milosevic as a politician, but Yugoslavia, yes. So those who had those elements in their hands, the national movement, the army, the League of Communists, the international solidarity, the NATO pact, the Warsaw treaty, which were then still existing, I'm talking about 1988, they could count that even without war, they could force their opponents to accept the political programme of Milosevic and the political programme was to recentralise Yugoslavia and to leave, abandon the constitution from 1974. However, the threat by such very powerful, predominant forces, did not work. The Slovenes, Slovenia, the League of Communists of Slovenia, was pretty aggressive, pretty fearless in its approach towards the army already in 1988. They went ahead with reforms quite bravely towards the abandonment of Communism and quite strongly came out against the policy of Serbia and the army. The leading forces in Croatia, the League of Communists of Croatia, took the position of waiting, not provoking, but also not providing, not giving strong resistance, thinking that Serbia and the army would give up the ultimate instrument, meaning war. But the masses were already quite heated up, there was a lot of nationalism, chauvinism. This is a state where normal human reasoning is lost, rational, normal, cool thinking does not function in the fire of nationalism. So as this mass rose up, it spontaneously also pulled the leadership into war, and this leadership didn't need much, and that's how the war broke out, which, as I would like to say again, is not really part of history. These are very recent events which a historian, according to the rules of his profession, should really not go into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilandzic, in these events, what was the role of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., its political structure, the elite, for 20 years before the war succeeded in emancipating itself from the federal political centre and functioned just like the other republics, Serbia and Croatia; namely, it's necessary to know that the first 20 years after the war, the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed to listen, to be obedient to the federal administration, but in the last 20 years, it won for itself the position which was similar to the position of Serbia, Croatia, and Slovenia in the sense of its identity, integrity, and individuality. In that sense, it was quite strong. When these events started that I am speaking about, there was the belief that the so-called anti-bureaucratic revolution, this is another name for the "happening of the people," so that the anti-bureaucratic revolution will spill over from Serbia into Bosnia-Herzegovina because there is about 31.3 percent of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, I think that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were really divided among themselves already in their daily life, from drinking coffee in a cafe or drinking a glass of water somewhere, they avoided Muslims -- Muslims, Serbs, and Croats avoided each other's company, avoided socialising, so that this mutual fear had the effect, or was acting also in the direction that they did not provoke one another in order not to start the fire. So that the streets, the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, tended towards spontaneous, unorganised, a tendency to put off the conflict until the emissaries came, started to come from Belgrade, both to Bosnia and to Croatia, to organise these people against, as it was said, separatist, anti-Yugoslav, anti-Communist forces in Croatia and Serbia. When these people sensed that Serbia will place themselves at their defence, including the possibility of war, they quickly accepted the appeal, the call, the invitation of the leadership. The military and Serbian leadership very quickly created its own parties, national parties, because you know in Yugoslavia, in the former Yugoslavia, Communist Yugoslavia, there were no other parties. When new parties started to appear, they were all down to one, they were nationalist, even chauvinist, aggressive, propelled by hate, the passion of hate, so that very quickly these parties were formed, Serbian, Croatian, and then after that, finally Muslim parties. As far as politics is concerned, of the other republics towards Bosnia, they are different from the ones conducted by Serbia. I stated yesterday that from the 1840s until the present day, Bosnia was defined in all documents of Serbia as Serbian land, and Croatia had at least three positions on Bosnia-Herzegovina in the course of history. Yesterday I spoke about how, in Austro-Hungary during the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian political elite supported the stance that it was better to hand Bosnia over to Serbia than to leave it under the rule of the Turks. The Croatian Communists were absolutely very hard-line supporters of the 1974 constitution and for the fact that Bosnia has to be preserved. The Croatian radical nationalists had absolute pretensions of ruling in Bosnia, but these forces are marginal, these are the remnants of the quisling independent state of Croatia which, as you know, was created by Hitler and Mussolini. In other words, the Croatian public opinion and the Croatian social policy was generally -- when I say "social," I mean it's an imprecise category, but we could say the public opinion, except the extreme radical nationalists, Croatia was in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state. And this, out of a fairly simple reason, namely, if, from a historical perspective the conflict between Croatia and Serbia was the fiercest conflict, similar to the conflict between Germany and France, and you know that in 70 years, three wars were conducted by Bismarck, Kaiser Wilhelm and Hitler. The conflict between Serbia and Croatia is similar, but until this last war, there was not -- such a conflict didn't actually take place, but Croatia, in the context of the conflict between itself and Serbia, has an ideal buffer, an ideal republic, an ideal state, which is called Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a vast mountain which divides -- separates two opponents which stand one facing the other but cannot jump over Bosnia and Herzegovina. From these geopolitical and historical reasons, the vast majority of the Croatian people is in favour of a stable sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. This has been the case for almost 100 years. However, the ultra nationalist option was aspiring for Bosnia-Herzegovina as Croatian land, and that is the ideology of the so-called Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, the national question in the former Yugoslavia and thereby in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, according to the views that you presented to us yesterday, is one of the very important disintegration factors in terms of the former Yugoslavia. Could you clarify on that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, because I spoke at length yesterday, the classes of citizenry that we, the Communists, used to call the bourgeoisie and the intelligentsia, are the protagonists of national ideas and national projects. However, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, from the mid-19th century onwards until the present day, history has shown that the bourgeoisie could not resolve the national question because, as I said, state ideas clashed. Perhaps you noted yesterday -- I don't know how clear I was, though -- but I tried to explain two key points as far as the resolution of the national issue in Yugoslavia is concerned. That is the point when, as the Habsburg monarchy fell apart, the southern Slavs of Austro-Hungary, who were about 8 million citizens, which is two times bigger than Serbia and Montenegro put together, established their own state. Now, what did I call it? The Slovenes, the Croats, and the Serbs, yes. That state, twice as big as Serbia and Montenegro, was a competitor to Serbia. So we had two southern Slav states which Serbia could not accept. With the support of the great powers of the entente, they broke up that state. The other point is the establishment of the Banovina of Croatia in 1939. So from this you can discern the silhouettes of three states: Slovenia, Croatia, and a Greater Serbia. But this was seven days before the Second World War broke out, so nothing could really be done. Now, the Communists come to the fore, the Communist party of Yugoslavia, and this is an historical paradox. The bourgeoisie cannot resolve the national question in Yugoslavia because they fight between themselves, they are imbued with nationalist ideologies. In comes a factor which is un-national, which is denying the existence of nations, for which nations is a foreign category. They have a globalist view of the world. For them, a national state is of no importance at all. The nation state is the product of capitalism; it is something foreign, it is something alien.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What nation state?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Any nation state. The Yugoslav, never mind. Croatian, nerve mind. Serbian, never mind. And what is important? The world proletarian revolution is important, Lenin's idea continues. According to the project of the Communist party of Yugoslavia and where we are going to place the borders between the future states is quite irrelevant. So it is precisely these kind of un-national nihilist thinkers or political ideologies who disregard and underestimate the existence of the nation state. They act as supra-national arbitrators that can reconcile the quarrelling nations and delineate their borders. Bearing in mind that they should delineate them in such a way that these peoples should follow the party that is going to resolve this for them. This is a globalist vision, this is a vision of Communists, and that is why the Communists were the only ones who were in a position to settle the conflict between the different nations of Yugoslavia and to create a federal community which functioned quite well until it was historically exhausted, rather, until the utopia of Communism was historically exhausted. It fell for different reasons, not because of the national question. As a vision, as a utopia, and particularly as a reality, it was unnatural because it trampled upon the individuality of the citizen, it turned the community into a god, and the citizen was nothing and that is why Communism failed. But I tried to explain that yesterday. The Communists, although they resolved the national question well in Yugoslavia, as they broke the Greater Serbian and Greater Croatian ideologies, they could not create a sound and stable society because as they intimately adhered to the hope and idea and the profound conviction that nations were withering away and that a socialist society would come into being, well, that was their mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, when I mentioned the national issue on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, I primarily wanted you to explain to us what the relations were between different nations in Yugoslavia. Were they homogenous? Were they in a state of conflict? Please compare the Serbian and Croatian nations on the one hand and, on the other hand, the relationship between these two nations and the Muslim nation.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: One cannot say, without getting a certain impression, that this was actually the continuing state of affairs in international relations in Yugoslavia. This was a very stratified thing. There was the period of the struggle against Stalin and Stalinism from 1948 until the 1960s, that was a rather monolithic period. There were times when certain nations or their elites, for practical reasons, kept quiet and even pretended that they had friendly relations with other nations, aware of the fact that in the given situations when the great powers were in favour of keeping Yugoslavia and, from 1918, from the very first days of Yugoslavia, the great powers were, on the whole, in favour of Yugoslavia, with the exception of Hitler's Germany. However, my basic premise is, and I think that it is valid, I think it is valid -- now, it is a question of proving it -- we can say that the main motto of the Serbian nation in Yugoslavia is the following: We are either in favour of a Greater Serbia and Yugoslavia or no Yugoslavia. Whereas the Croats thought the following: We are in favour of a federal or confederal Yugoslavia or no Yugoslavia at all. So this is a clash of two state ideas, two visions which co-existed in the hope, for a certain period of time, that a compromise would be found. Would it be possible to reach a compromise? It seemed possible at given points in time. I tried to explain that yesterday. You see, the Serbs in Yugoslavia are not like Russians in the USSR. Russians were the majority people in the USSR, Serbs were 36 percent of the population in Yugoslavia, and, in addition to that, the centre, from a civilisational, cultural, and industrial point of view, was not in Serbia but in Croatia and in Slovenia, so these two nations are more developed than the Serbian nation which makes it difficult for Serbia to play a leading role, a role of hegemony. There is a kind of balance of power. So, for example, when King Alexander imposed his dictatorship, a pro-fascist dictatorship, if we can call it that, it is interesting that the Yugoslav idea of fascism did not succeed. Why? This was not the case of Germany. The German people could have one Fuhrer, the Spanish people could have one Caudillo, the Italian people could have one Duce, but in Yugoslavia, you could not find that kind of a single person, it cannot be the King. Why? Because within six nations, you cannot find one person who will be the Fuhrer. So in Yugoslavia, parliamentarianism cannot function either because it suits Serbia. Can you not establish fascism because fascism grows on the premise that there is one nation only and that was not the case of Yugoslavia. So that is why it continued to exist with this kind of balance of power that I mentioned and also with the support of the international community. In this context, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a special case which contributed -- how should I put this? -- to Yugoslavia and its life in several directions. First of all, during the Second World War, this was the fortress of Tito's army together with Croatia. It is these two republics that were the mainstays of the partisan war because we saw yesterday that after three months in 1941, the partisan movement was defeated in Serbia. After the war, Bosnia and Herzegovina was exploited as the Yugoslav Ruhr because it had many mineral resources. Serbs and Croats -- I tried to explain this yesterday -- in this republic, they accepted what the Second World War brought forth. There was no other way out because the Greater Serbian idea and the Greater Croatian idea was defeated in Bosnia because Bosnia was the land that was supposed to belong either to a Greater Croatia or to a Greater Serbia, and since the Communist movement broke this up, this was no longer the case. As far as Muslims are concerned, they were a rather strong pillar of support of the Yugoslav -- I'm not going to call it Unitarian concept, I'm not going to call it that, but of Titoism, if that is what we are going to call it, of the constitution of 1974. They supported that until they came to realise that this could not remain as such, that -- they realised that Croatia and Slovenia were leaving Yugoslavia, and if they were to stay, they would have the same status as Albanians in Kosovo, and I think that was of decisive importance when Izetbegovic decided to seek a referendum and independence. There is one more thing I have to add. Until this war, Croats and Muslims were, you know, whatever a person says before this Honourable Court has another side to it, so one has to choose one's words very carefully. Not in order to avoid an answer but because of the complexity of the situation involved. What am I trying to say? The Muslims and the Croats were political allies from the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina until -- until this last war. Political allies. But, on the other hand, at the same time, in a way, culturally, civilisationally, religiously, they were alienated from each other. They did not live together. They did not live close to one another. These were two communities which had political interests. They were threatened by Greater Serbian ideas, so they were close to each other politically but at an intimate level, so to speak, their lives were separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When speaking of the political alliance between the Croats and Muslims throughout history from the annexation of Bosnia into the Austro-Hungarian empire and until the recent war that was waged in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the best of my knowledge, this fits within your thesis that a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina always suited Croatia except for this extremist minority precisely for that reason, and those were probably the reasons why there was political cooperation with the Bosnian Muslims. Is that thesis correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I think it is correct. Although I cannot go into this, what happened later, but if we are judging history, yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When speaking about this national question of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, is it true that actually the essence of the national question from the very inception of Yugoslavia, that is to say, 70 years ago, and practically until these recent events, that this was, in fact, a smouldering conflict between the Serbs and Croats in this area for quite a period of time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I just add one more thing. You have probably heard of a phenomena such as a greater France, a greater Germany, greater Bulgaria, Greater Serbia, greater, greater, greater. There is not a single nation, once it is born, I mean, there is no need to explain what a nation is, but there is not a single nation that does not aspire for a sovereign state. This is the 19th century I'm talking about. And this national phenomenon is something that destroyed Europe, after all. If you look at the French revolution, for example, you could hardly find a German who would say that he was a German. But in 1848, when this spring of nations came to the fore, then, in the mid 19th century, everything somehow moved into nationalism. After all, you know, Europe lost world leadership because of these nationalisms that were exhausting one another, that led to bloodshed in the first world war and the Second World War. It is nationalism that stood behind all of this, primarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, when you explained to us yesterday and today from a historiographer's point of view of the events in Yugoslavia, you said that in that area, there were always two fundamental processes, one was one of integration and one was of disintegration. Could you just tell us to what extent did these processes prevail over one another over the past 70 years?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer this question without falling into oversimplified explanations. Very often, nations and peoples do not what they wish but what they have to do, and often they work against themselves while thinking that they are working for themselves. What am I trying to say? I said that most of the southern Slavs lived within the Austro-Hungarian empire, the Croats for about 900 years and they were under Vienna and Budapest although they had the status of an autonomous kingdom. But they hoped that as they get out of this monarchy, there would be fraternal relations with Serbia, and at a given point of time, they got carried away. They thought it was possible. However, this did not turn out to be the case, and there was disintegration. The Communists claimed that they had established fraternity and unity among all the nations of Yugoslavia and that this was the most monolithic state on the planet because, until yesterday, people were killing one another and now they turned into brothers who have expressed a high degree of solidarity from various points of view. But if I were to simplify things to the end, I could say that Yugoslavia was included and excluded, included into and excluded from, smaller or bigger European integration. For example, from 1918 until 1941, it was an element of the European Versailles system. From 1941 to 1945, these lands were part of Hitler's new order. From 1945 onwards, Yugoslavia shared the fate of others, rather that it had to adjust to blocs, although it was a non-bloc country. So these two blocs kept it alive. When this European structure collapsed from Berlin to Vladivostok, Kamchatka, the Kuril Islands. I don't know, when the entire empire fell apart. At that point the external forces that kept it together fell apart, but without the collapse of the Soviet empire, without Gorbachev and Yeltsin, I doubt that the disintegration forces in Yugoslavia could have won the establishment of independent states, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia. I doubt it. So the main determining factor which governed the entire life of Yugoslavia was the international one, after all. But disintegration forces became stronger in the process. It is wrong to think that Croatian separatists, that Croatian separatists are the main disintegrating force. That is wrong. I mean, they are a disintegrating force but they are not the main disintegrating force. If you are to read new versions of the history of Yugoslavia today and the new versions of the history of Serbia in Belgrade, they have proclaimed that Yugoslavia was the greatest tragedy of the Serb people. Dobrica Cosic, a man who enjoys the reputation as the father of the nation, he said that Serbia strangled itself in 1918 as it entered Yugoslavia. Why? Because as it entered Yugoslavia, it lost its identity, and it gave itself to a utopia, and therefore did not manage to have a respectable state of its own in this area. Milan Nedic, Serbia’s main quisling in the Second World War, also wrote about this, that the creation of Yugoslavia was a tragedy for the Serb people. So it is not only the Croatian separatists can be blamed for everything. I think that they are even of a lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I wish to observe the rules that you have set this morning, perhaps this would be an appropriate point to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to continue at 40 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please excuse us for the delay, but as I did mention, we had a meeting with the Deputy of the Under Secretary of the United Nations, and that is why we are a little late. Mr. Mikulicic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, you mentioned and you spoke about the disintegration processes which were taking place in the last 70 years in the territory of Yugoslavia; sometimes stronger, sometimes weaker, but always present. In your opinion as a history expert and from the point of today's distance, was it essential that Yugoslavia disintegrated in the way that it has done, meaning that a war had to happen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: This is a problem that is on the minds of all the political elites, the scientists, the peoples of former Yugoslavia, whether war could be avoided. Historians should not give a decisive answer to this question because social processes which differ from natural processes, cases cannot repeat themselves, so that is why it is very difficult to answer this question. But with certain reserves, I would say the following: The conflict between Serbia and the Yugoslav army on one side, and Croatia and Slovenia and other republics on the other side, came about for two reasons: First, the Serb people found themselves before a dilemma in 1989-1990, that Yugoslavia could possibly break up. They faced the dilemma then, i.e. the conviction, that with the break-up of Yugoslavia, the results of the First and Second Balkan Wars from the First and Second World Wars would be cancelled out because these wars had brought a fourfold increase of the territories under the control, especially between the two World Wars, under the control of Serbia. This spectre, this vision that the victims of four previous wars would be cancelled out, was a very powerful force acting in order to prevent the disintegration of Yugoslavia. Secondly, the branches of the Serbian people are strong in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was about 570.000 Serbs in Croatia and in Bosnia 1.310.000 people. In the event of a break-up of Yugoslavia, according to the consciousness, the understanding of the Serbian leadership, these people, or this part of the Serbian people, would come under the regime of independent states and they would be threatened. So these are two reasons that very powerfully affected Serbia and its wish to prevent, at any cost, the break-up of Yugoslavia, not only the break-up but also to prevent the abandoning of the constitution of 1974 because that constitution of 1974 was confederative. So in order to prevent this, to prevent the break-up of Yugoslavia, the only way was to revitalise the Communist composition, because this was ideal, it is the best, the most functional mechanism of control over society, regardless of what kind of a society that is. In history, it had shown itself to be as ideal for control of society, Communism, so that it was pre-determined that Serbia and the JNA must, on one side, support the Communist system and then, on the other hand, prevent democratisation because democratisation in itself leads at least towards confederation. So, for example, that is why Serbia wanted the prime minister of the federal government, Ante Markovic, to be replaced because he did have very strong support from the United States which believed that democratisation -- or that it would preserve Yugoslavia by transferring it over to a Western democratic regime. This was the concept of the prime minister, and this was what was also rejected. On the other hand, Slovenia and Croatia had a growing movement in order to achieve two goals: to gain as much independence as possible, confederation at least, on the one hand, and then, on the other hand, to cross over into Western parliamentarianism which did not suit Serbia. So these are these two concepts which are mutually conflicting and which led to war. These are theses which could be defended. What is difficult to explain and to defend is the fact of why the international community did not wake up in time in order to prevent this war and, secondly, why democratic forces within Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia, Macedonia did not join together against the forces of war. This is pretty difficult to explain. If democratic liberal parties of all the peoples of Yugoslavia had joined into an alliance, and this was the idea of the federal government headed by Markovic, with the support of the international community, the war possibly could have been avoided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But under the circumstances, when the attempt by Ante Markovic failed, in such a situation, when Slobodan Milosevic came to power in Serbia, and you said earlier that he had a vast machine supporting him, in such a situation and taking into account the ideas which the then Serbian leadership declared, in your opinion, in such circumstances was war inevitable or perhaps not inevitable?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to reply to that question. Yes and no. I am not avoiding an answer, but it is difficult to answer that question because an irrational situation was created, a situation of euphoria, a situation where the masses and the leaderships tended towards conflict. I think the opponents of Milosevic, extreme opponents, also very easily -- easily hoped for a solution without war, and this is an irrational situation where a normal political mind disappears. Still, I am more prone to the thesis that the army, which was a party army, you know that the army was the so-called seventh republic in Yugoslavia. The representative of the army was always a member of the presidency of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the Communist party of Yugoslavia. Each republic had its representative at the leadership of the Communist party. The army had its own representative. It had the status of a so-called republican party organisation, separate for 50 years from society, exclusively tied to Tito, ideologically very indoctrinated, brought up on anti-liberalism, and the conviction that Western imperialism is the only enemy of Yugoslavia, except in the period of the conflict with the USSR. So that the Defence Ministers, Mamula, Kadijevic, and their statements are taken from interviews and written directives for the army, are full of the thesis that Western imperialism is anti-Communist, anti-socialist, anti-Yugoslav. The war plans of the Yugoslav People's Army were always made, except maybe until 1969-1970, were always made with the supposition that an attack on Yugoslavia is only possible from the West so that the army, until the end, remained an ideological army which has supreme value to the state of Yugoslavia and to Communism. So this coincided with the leadership in Serbia and an alliance was made between these two main factors and they went into war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has finished its questions and passes the word to the learned colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have listened with interest to your presentation which, I must say, I found very balanced. Just touching on the last question that you raised there. I agree with you that the JNA was committed to preservation of Yugoslavia. But would you agree with me, during the course of 1991, that it was less committed to that cause and more committed to a Serbian cause?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I will try to respond. The military leadership, until the summer of 1991, was more in favour of Yugoslavia. However, you probably heard the President of Yugoslavia, his name was Jovic, he was a Serb, he published a book on the disintegration of Yugoslavia; and at a dramatic moment, there was a conflict, a verbal conflict, between the military leadership and the Serbian leadership. The Serbian leadership said, told Kadijevic and the Chief of the General Staff Adzic, "Let Slovenia go, let a part of Croatia go. Place yourselves in the regions held by Serbs in Croatia and we will defend a new Yugoslavia, a third Yugoslavia, which will comprise Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Vojvodina, of course Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a part of the territory of Croatia populated by Serbs." So Adzic then said, "So you are breaking up Yugoslavia. I will arrest you now," he told them. But when the army had its debacle in Slovenia on the 27th of June in 1991, when their action was a failure, it failed, I think it was compromised as a military power, and having seen that without Serbia it cannot really go on further with this idea of preserving the entire Yugoslavia, sometime in those days it definitely crossed over to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that would be evidenced by the fact that when it left Slovenia, it did so in such a way that it really had no intentions of returning, and I speak of the JNA. That would be right, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think, as an historian you would agree with me that armies are the sorts of creatures that require political leadership, and that with the breakdown of the presidency in Yugoslavia, the army found itself without political leadership and it turned to Milosevic as its political leader; would you agree with that as a statement? I speak in the period of 1991.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that certainly from the perspective of President Milosevic, there was no doubt in his mind that he had captured the control of the army, of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, another area that I would like to talk about is, you spoke of the historical attempts at compromise between the very disparate interests of both Croatia and Serbia. Was another such attempt at that compromise a meeting that was held at Karadjordjevo on the 10th and 11th of March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you permit, the Defence objects to the Prosecutor's question because this question exceeds the framework of the testimony of Professor Bilandzic as the expert about the historical events which preceded the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. These events that my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, would like to ask questions about are part of another area which is not the subject of the testimony of our expert witness, and the Defence did not ask him any questions about that. So that in this way, the Prosecution exceeds the expertise of the witness, Professor Bilandzic, with their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I respond to that, Your Honour? Your Honours, cross-examination is a matter at large. If a witness comes before the court and can assist the court in matters which are known to the witness and he can comment upon or if the Prosecutor or Defence counsel wish to embark upon some line of questioning which is relevant to the issues at hand, in my submission it is not appropriate to merely say cross-examination should be limited only to those matters raised in the course of testimony. I have reason to believe that the Professor can assist us with some of the answers to these two questions, and it touches upon matters which, in the course of my closing address, I will urge upon Your Honours are important in understanding the conflict that ultimately developed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So for those reasons, Your Honours, I submit that the line of questioning is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Professor Bilandzic said that this whole question is very complex and it is hard to stay exclusively within the framework of the facts because events have a certain internal dynamic and they become part of a system, so I think that the Defence will have the opportunity later to ask more questions, if they so wish. So the Trial Chamber accepts this question. Mr. Niemann, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, do you wish me to repeat the question or do you remember it sufficiently to answer it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have any information about Karadjordjevo, but as far as I know from the media, that accord or non-accord was never published anywhere, as far as I know. This matter between these two in Karadjordjevo, they discussed the division of Bosnia. As far as I know, there are no documents about that, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. I know you weren't in attendance at the meeting, but you did perform a function as a consequence of that meeting, did you not, in terms of representing Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I have to say that there's a lot of mystification about this. This is a conversation among several people, intellectuals of Serbia and Croatia, the main topic of which was whether war can be avoided and how it can be avoided. Since I was absolutely against any kind of division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I obstructed that idea that it should be discussed, and that whole conversation came down to the problem of whether both sides recognised the results of the people's liberation war and the socialist revolution. These results are the decisions of Avnoj in 1943, the decisions of the five constitutions and the constitution of 1974. Since the Serb side negated the validity of the Avnoj decisions from 1943 and particularly the constitution of 1974, I withdrew from the group. At that time, I was already retired. I did teach at the faculty, but only in the graduate school. So I have to say that a debate was conducted similar to the debate today where the central question is whether one should adhere or not to the decisions of Avnoj and the constitution of 1974. So I repeat that my very decisive stance, that as soon as I saw that the expert group from Serbia had that stance, I withdrew from those talks, and I never took part again in any kind of talks about the eventual division of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Professor, it is a fact, isn't it, that there was a meeting between Presidents Milosevic and Tudjman in Karadjordjevo, and it is a fact that as a consequence of that, a commission was established, a commission made up of representatives from both Croatia and Serbia, to draw up plans on how Bosnia could be divided? There's no question about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I repeat that a group, Croatian group -- and I did have influence there to a large part -- absolutely refused the continuation of any kind of talks concerning the violations of inter-republic boundaries and which concerned the validity of the decisions of Avnoj and the 1974 constitution. Things ended there. I resigned from the continuation of the talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you shouldn't think that I'm in any way attacking your integrity. I know that you resigned and I know that you were concerned about the fate of the Muslims and that you made this known to the political leadership at the time. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I publicly came out against the radicalism, both Serb and Croatian, because, as I know, for 50 years I was a Communist, and I didn't accept the concepts about the division, so that's why I resigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In no way do I imply any criticism of you. I am merely endeavouring to elicit the facts. But the fact of the matter is that following the meeting between Presidents Tudjman and Milosevic, you were assigned, as a member of this commission, to endeavour to reach agreement with the Serbs on a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that your concern at the time was the fate of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I saw what was happening, from kind of historical curiosity, I accepted to take part in the talks. But as soon as I saw the stands which do not recognise the achievements of the people's liberation war and the national revolution, I refused to participate further. That is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. You did go so far, though, as to give your views on the fact that the Muslims would be the victims of any such division, but those views weren't accepted, were they, by the political leadership of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Actually, when I was resigning, I said that I could not take part in this undertaking, and I cannot say what happened afterwards because contacts probably continued. But through other people, probably more direct, probably through diplomatic channels or directly -- I'm really not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I accept fully, having heard you give your testimony, that you could have participated in this exercise of the commission without fully appreciating the consequences, and then, very honourably, you resigned from it when you did. But the reality is that it was a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina between Serbia and Croatia, wasn't it? That was the plan?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, bear in mind that this was about three or four months before the war, and in my own mind, I thought that this was a game of delay tactics because, in my mind, this was so irrational that intimately I could not believe it, that this was their true intention. First of all, I think they wanted to gain time and delay the conflict between Croatia and the JNA in Serbia and, in a way, some kind of political cunning. I repeat, this was irrational for me, so that's why I gave up on the whole thing. What happened afterwards, what kind of ideas were presented, how this process evolved further, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, perhaps unwittingly but very sadly the international community itself further contributed to the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't it, because the Vance-Owen Plan, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, was something which more or less accorded with what was hoped and intended as a consequence of the Karadjordjevo meeting in 1991; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I would say that the international community either unwittingly or quite consciously gave rise to the conflict, but let me tell you how. The basic premise of President Bush and of the European Community was the following: We are in favour of the unity of Yugoslavia but with the right to self-determination. That was it, more or less. Those forces, that is to say, Milosevic and the JNA that were in favour of keeping Yugoslavia, only came to accept the first part of the sentence: We are in favour of maintaining the unity of Yugoslavia. Full stop. But that is not a full stop. There was a comma. But we are also in favour of the right to self-determination. Those forces that wanted to get out of Yugoslavia, they simply deleted the first part of the sentence, "We are in favour of unity," et cetera, and they only took the other part of the phrase, "We are in favour of the right to self-determination." So with this kind of -- how should I put this? -- this possibility of double interpretation, every side sought some kind of support for their plans. For example, the prime minister of the federal government precisely counted on that kind of attitude of the international community, but then others were counting on the right to self-determination, which is legal and legitimate, according to international standards. You see, as far as the Vance-Owen Plan is concerned, it is still not clear to me whether the international community and the European Union, Vance and Owen, did they really support the division of Bosnia? It is hard to believe, in my opinion, because, to my mind, this is not humane, this is not wise, and it would be hard for me to believe that these people lightheartedly accepted this. It's possible, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here, Professor, a quote from a television programme which you appeared on, and I have the video, so if you would like to see it, please ask me and I'll show it to you. But you are --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are seen on the programme. When speaking of the Vance-Owen Plan, you said this, and I'll read it out and just ask whether you agree that that's what you said. When asked about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, you said: "After they signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, the Croats from Herzegovina thought that the division was done." I think you're speaking of them. "We have been given our mini-state of Herceg-Bosna. We can do whatever we want there. We can rename the streets, we can rename the University of Mostar, and Mostar can, at last, be our capital. They thought the battle was over, but they were wrong." I don't ask you whether you agree with them because we know you have made it very clear that you don't agree with the fact that that may be the case. But do you agree with me that's what you said? And is that your belief, that the Vance-Owen Plan did give those people, those Croat people in Herceg-Bosna, that belief?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: The context is exactly what you mentioned, that is criticism of a certain kind of behaviour. But I always thought that this would never actually happen. This is criticism. This is a warning: Don't go that way. That was the intention of that interview. That was the context. A critical attitude towards the policy of the international community and a critical attitude towards the behaviour of the people in Herceg-Bosna. Warning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sadly, Professor, all that you said came to be true.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: (Nods)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question in order to clarify the time framework of the events that have just been discussed. Re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, when speaking of the meeting in Karadjordjevo, could you please tell us what the time context is in terms of the events in Bosnia that happened. Was it before the war or before the republics of the former Yugoslavia attained their independence, so could you please give us the time reference?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: This was the time of negotiations between the heads of republics. I don't know how many meetings they had, at least six but possibly even ten public meetings as they were moving the venue of these meetings from Titograd, namely Podgorica in Montenegro and then Bled in Slovenia and then they went to Ohrid, Macedonia, so they were going all over the place in order to find compromises to how they could resolve the Yugoslav crisis. As far as the recognition of states is concerned, this was nine or ten months before the recognition of these states, so this was a period of time when an effort was being made to avoid conflict and war and to save peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, did this meeting, which was one of a series of meetings, while the former Yugoslavia was still formally in existence, can we interpret this as one of the many attempts to try to resolve this by an accommodation of views?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: That interpretation can be accepted but, to the best of my knowledge, exactly what they agreed upon never came out into broad daylight, so we don't really know. I literally have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But will you agree with the claim that, in terms of time, this was nine or ten months before the former republics of Yugoslavia attained their sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes, yes, nine months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Professor Bilandzic, the Chamber doesn't have any further questions to put to you. The Criminal Tribunal wishes to thank you for having come here and for having brought your information to us, and we wish you a safe return to your country. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must admit that I am impressed by the professional and human atmosphere before this Honourable Court, and I must say that I have excellent impressions of the moments that I spent with you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber always tries to create a human and cooperative atmosphere because I think that this is the right path for seeing that justice is done. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I be excused? I have the other Chamber to go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In this situation, now that we have finished the statement of the expert witness, Professor Bilandzic, earlier, before we thought it would, before the Defence thought, I must say at this point in time we don't have further witnesses for the Defence. When the Defence was planning this, we were supposed to have three days for this part of the trial, and we thought that Professor Bilandzic would need about three days. However, we worked more expeditiously than the Defence could have imagined. So for this week, we don't have any further witnesses. When we meet next time, we are going to have more witnesses of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber wishes to thank you for having made all these efforts and for having done your best to make our work efficient and well-coordinated. It is clear to us that it is difficult to calculate precisely how much time one needs. We are going to adjourn now until the 15th of June. I wish you a good weekend and wish success in their work to all those who are present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 11.36 a.m. to be reconvened on 15 June 1998 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
